chapter_theme: Manimidai pavalam 201-220: friends answer women left for the desert road, mothers of eloped daughters grieve, friends press lovers from night meetings toward marriage, and puram fame (Alankanam, Ori's Kolli, Eyinan's fall, Mathi's ford, Chellur) serves as the measure of gossip and beauty.

201.reading: The friend asks the grieving woman why she despairs that gossip has filled the common ground like the sea swelling at full moon off the Pandya's Korkai and that her mother lies sleepless and sighing: the man who crossed the long summer desert, where a male bear sports with his she-bear and their cub on the hill slope, would not settle there even if he were given the rich rice country of the Cholas.
201.nuance: The friend first repeats the woman's own complaint (lines 1 to 11) and only then answers it, so the gossip and the mother's sighing are given in the woman's voice. The comfort rests on a hyperbole of refusal (not even the Chola land) rather than on a promise of his return date.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend comforts a woman whose man has crossed the summer desert

comparisons.tenor: the gossip that has filled the common ground
the thick fur of the bear cub

iraicchi.act: the male bear stays and sports with his she-bear, whose cub is with them, on the hill slope of the desert road
iraicchi.sense: the man who saw even the bear keep to its mate and young on that road will not stay away from his own woman

202.reading: The friend tells the lover who leaves after a night meeting that in his hill, where a wounded tusker that beat off a tiger lifts its trunk and sighs among its young she-elephants and the vengai blossoms fly up like a smith's sparks onto the dark bushes, she wonders whether anyone but themselves suffers as they do while he comes at midnight, spear for company, down the dark stony path where thunder splits the hooded snake.
202.nuance: The question 'are there others besides us?' turns the women's fear for him into pressure to marry: the colophon says she is urging marriage, and the poem does it only by counting the dangers. A traditional reading takes the wounded tusker among its she-elephants as the lover who braves the night to reach the girl; it is left as scene here because only one correspondence (danger overcome) is clear.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக் குறிக்கண் வந்து நீங்கும் தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: a lover comes to the night meeting through the hill path

comparisons.tenor: the vengai blossoms settling on the dark bushes

203.reading: The mother whose daughter has eloped says that she kept silent when the gossiping women told her day after day what the girl was doing, sparing her shame, but the girl feared her mother would know and left with her spear-bearing young man across the hills; may it prove that she was not such a mother, and may she herself be the housewife of the lonely hill hamlet with its nochi hedge who takes the girl in as a passing guest when she arrives safe.
203.nuance: Her wish is not that the girl come back but that she be the stranger on the road who shelters her: a mother's care transferred to the place the daughter has chosen. Her silence, meant as kindness, is what the daughter read as danger, so the poem turns on a misunderstanding between them.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has left with her lover across the desert hills

204.reading: The man, his work done in the Pandya's great camp, tells his charioteer that the evening of the rains has come over the grassland, with bee swarms humming at the fragrant mullai, so he must drive fast to reach the shoulders of his bright-bangled wife, whose hair smells like the groves of Vaanan's Sirukudi where the reapers' drums scare birds from the flowered pools.
204.nuance: The season he promised to return in has arrived on its own (உதுக்காண் வந்தன்று பொழுதே), so his haste is the keeping of a word. The camp opens with the king's world-shading umbrella and sea-like army; the close sets that public scene against a farming village's fragrance in his wife's hair.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains, the grassland and the jasmine evening of return

comparisons.tenor: the fragrance of the wife's hair

205.reading: The woman tells the friend who urges her to bear up that her lover, who swore with a lying heart that he would never leave her, like those joined in an old flawless friendship of mingled lives, has gone and left her weeping; even so, may he easily gain wealth enough to feed guests in a house as rich as Killi's Kaveri port, as he crosses the hill path of strange speech in the cool season where an elephant's musth runs and the male monkey calls and leaps on the high branch.
205.nuance: The reproach and the blessing come in one breath: she names his oath a lie and still wishes his errand success, and what she wishes him is wealth for hospitality, the householder's duty, not riches for himself.

thinai_evidence.note: he has left her to cross the desert for wealth

comparisons.vehicle: உயிர்கலந்து ஒன்றிய தொன்றுபடு நட்பின் செயிர்தீர் நெஞ்சமொடு செறிந்தோர்
comparisons.tenor: the lover as he spoke his promise
the rich house she wishes him

206.reading: The woman, refusing the go-between, asks her friend what this will be called: the lord of a town where small boys climb the dark back of a buffalo whose twisted horns spread as ludicrously as a dancer's gestures, looking from afar like monkeys on a boulder, delights in marrying women with mango-sprout skin in his festive city, and sulking at it her broad soft shoulders have melted like the salt heaps of Veerai in heavy rain.
206.nuance: The mockery is in the image: the great buffalo carries boys about like a toy and looks absurd, and so does he, ridden by every woman. Her own body, not her words, gives the refusal its force: the shoulders that waste like rained-on salt.

colophon.thurai: வாயில் வேண்டிச் சென்றவிறலிக்குத் தலைமகள் வாயில் மறுத்து.

thinai_evidence.note: she sulks at the husband's new marriages

comparisons.tenor: the spreading twisted horns of the buffalo
the boys on the buffalo's back seen from afar
the skin of the women he marries

comparisons.vehicle: நெடுவெள் உப்பின் நிரம்பாக் குப்பை பெரும் பெயற்கு உருகி யா அங்கு

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the women who make free with him

pairs.situation: lesser women climb onto the man as boys climb the buffalo
the town sees it from afar and names it (என்னெனப் படுங்கொல்)

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the buffalo of her own marutham town, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

207.reading: The mother whose daughter eloped wonders whether the girl, who refused with a sick heart the sweet milk mixed with honey that her mother held out while combing her hair and coaxing her, has drunk, sighing and with sweat on her crescent brow, the brackish pot of water her heartless lover drew from a well dug where a sun-scorched tusker had rolled, on the dread forked desert path cut by the hooves of the salt traders' grey donkeys.
207.nuance: The road is built from the salt trade, carried from the sea to the western uplands, so the desert here is a merchant road, not wild land. The poem's last image is of the girl at home refusing milk, so the mother's question about the well water is also about the comfort she failed to give.

thinai_evidence.note: the scorched desert road the girl has taken

208.reading: The lover, leaving after their meeting, blesses the girl of fine dark hair, fragrant as the flowers of Ori's Kolli, who came and gave herself with a desire that shame could not hold back, like a flood the salt-pan bank cannot stop and like Akuthai who brought back the kin after the outcry of the Vel women when Aay Eyinan fell to Minjili at Paazhi and Nannan would not look on the field.
208.nuance: Most of the poem is a puram story told inside a single simile: Eyinan the generous, killed at noon, the birds that should have shaded him, Nannan's refusal to see. What it measures is the girl's boldness, a thing usually blamed in akam, here blessed. Line 18 (அகுதை கிளைதந்தாங்கு) is obscure, and the turn of the Nannan episode is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero rejoices after a secret union

comparisons.vehicle: வசைவிடக் கடக்கும் வயங்குபெருந் தானை அகுதை கிளைதந் தாங்கு

comparisons.tenor: her desire that shame could not hold

209.reading: The friend tells the woman not to weep that her shoulders have lost their beauty, her mother grieves and the gossip is louder than the roar at Alankanam when Chezhiyan beat the seven: though her man has gone beyond Pulli's Vengadam, he cannot forget her beauty, which is like the statue set up by the god on Kolli, the hill Kaari of Mullur gave to the Cheras after killing Ori.
209.nuance: The friend first speaks the woman's complaint in her own words and then answers it, as in 201. Both measures in the poem come from puram: a Pandya victory for the gossip, a Kolli statue that outlived the change of its lords for her beauty, which is the friend's point: his love will last as the statue did.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the rocky land beyond Vengadam

comparisons.vehicle: கொல்லி நிலைபெறு கடவுள் ஆக்கிய பலர்புகழ் பாவை

210.reading: The friend, knowing the lover stands by unseen, tells the woman that the lord of the shore, where a great fish struck by the fishermen's harpoon stains the sea with its blood, arcs through the waves like a rainbow and follows the boats with its strength gone, once came at midnight thinking of her shoulders and praised their seaside grove endlessly, and now, they hear, says the screw-pine thickets block his chariot and the way is hard.
210.nuance: The friend sets his first praise of their shore against his present excuse about the same shore, and lets him overhear the comparison. The wounded fish that still follows the boats is sometimes read as a hidden image of a lover hurt yet clinging; it is left as scene because its matching to the people is not fixed by the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen, the seaside grove and screw-pine

comparisons.tenor: the wounded fish arcing through the waves

211.reading: The friend, seeing the woman changed, tells her that though her man is in the land of strange speech beyond Vengadam, where a tusker rubbing against the maraam scatters its lime-white blossoms like hail onto the rock where farmers dry their rice seed, he will be kind and return, he who left her weeping with gossip roaring like the water at Mathi's stony ford, where Ezhini's teeth were set into the gate of Venmani.
211.nuance: The gossip is again measured by a war story, here a grim trophy: a fallen raider's teeth driven into a fortress door. Lines 9 to 15 compress the Ezhini episode so tightly that its sequence (the cattle, the outcry, the king's command) cannot be fixed.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்டதலைமகளது வேறுபாடு கண்டு தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone to a far land leaving her in tears

212.reading: The lover, after a meeting that failed, curses his heart: desiring a girl whose beauty is like a golden statue holding the young sunlight, whose teeth are like the shoots of reed tubers in sand and whose speech is like the music of a lute played in sevvazhi, it never thought she was hard to win and crossed the bitter waste every day, bringing him endless pain; may its keen pride be broken as the sea was when Kuttuvan's tempered spear drove it back.
212.nuance: The curse runs through a puram image, the Chera who besieged the ocean itself; the heart's pride is set against the sea's, and both are pierced. Line 9 (the water troubled by the elephant herd) is unclear in its connection.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover's longing for a girl who is hard to meet

comparisons.vehicle: தாஇல் நன்பொன் தைஇய பாவை விண்தவழ் இளவெயிற் கொண்டுநின் றன்ன
நாணற் கிழங்கு மணற்கு ஈன்ற முளைஓ ரன்ன

213.reading: The friend tells the woman that though her man chose to cross the shadeless waterless waste beyond the Tondaiyar's Vengadam, into the land of the Vadugar who wear wilted athiral in their curly hair and offer toddy to the cattle they raid, he will not linger there even if he were given the world of the worthy together with its nectar, forgetting to join her shoulders like the bamboo of Kolli and her hair rippled like Kaveri sand.
213.nuance: The friend's hyperbole goes past any kingdom to heaven itself: not even the gods' world and its nectar outweighs the woman's embrace. The road is drawn from its people, a raiding folk with their own rites, which makes the distance cultural as well as physical.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless, shadeless desert he crossed

comparisons.tenor: the gems shining in the field

214.reading: In the war camp, where the rain pours ceaselessly from a sky that has hidden the day, chilling the elephant herds, and the king, eager for glory, does not sleep, the man tells his heart that the war is their duty, and asks how she of thick hair, who knew him as her own, will fare as she hears alone in the rainy evening the sad sevvazhi lute and the flute of cowherds driving home cattle with bells.
214.nuance: The colophon gives the speech to the woman, but the speaker is in the camp and says the war is ours (அமரும் நம்வயினதுவே), so it can only be the man; he imagines her evening, not his own. The music that wounds her is his invention, placed in her hearing.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains, the evening and the cowherds of the waiting season

215.reading: The friend tells the man, who stands ready with spear in hand to cross the hills for work in a land of other tongues, that wishing him a swift and successful going would be well enough for those who could bear to stay behind grieving for the absent, on a road where bowmen who bite the finger that missed its mark raise dread stone heaps over men they kill and a red-beaked male vulture picks the eyes from the heads of corpses and drops them for his mate.
215.nuance: The blessing is withheld by a conditional: it would be fine to say 'go well', but only to someone able to stay behind, which the woman is not. The vulture feeding its mate is the poem's sharpest stroke: on a road of killing, even the carrion bird provides for its partner without leaving her.

colophon.thurai: செலவுணர்த்திய தோழி தலைமகள் குறிப்பறிந்து தலைமகனைச் செலவழுங்குவித்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the robbers' road of stone heaps and vultures

iraicchi.act: the male vulture gathers what it finds on the killing ground and brings it to its mate
iraicchi.sense: even the vulture of that road provides for its mate without leaving her, so the man need not part from his wife to provide

216.reading: The courtesan, speaking so that the wife's women will hear, says the wives of the lord of the cool-ford town, where a bard's daughter fishes with a fine rod and roasts the varaal on vanji wood for her toddy-drinking father, are said to talk of her as they please; if she is caught in that gossip, so be it, but if she goes to their street they will suffer like the great tusker when the Chelli lord's white spear struck Aathan Ezhini's chest.
216.nuance: Her threat is to visit, not to fight; she makes her mere presence in their street a wound. The simile's referents are uncertain: whether the suffering tusker is Ezhini's own elephant or Ezhini himself called a tusker cannot be settled from the line.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகட்குப் பாங்காயினார் கேட்பத் தனக்குப் பாங்காயினார்க்குப் பரத்தை சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the courtesan's quarrel with the wives of the town's lord

217.reading: Told of the coming parting, the woman says that now the cold season has come, with white rain-clouds like carded cotton, cane flowers swaying, pakandrai blooming white, avarai and thondri opening, herons crying in every field and women at the ford shivering without their ornaments, she will proclaim to every couple 'whatever wealth you gain, do not part', for her body is ruined by the lover who took her beauty and left, and she shivers in the hard cold with chattering teeth.
217.nuance: Her answer to news of his going is a public maxim addressed to all lovers, made from her own case. The long catalogue of the cold season is not decoration: every flower and bird marks the time he should be home, and the women shivering at the ford are a picture of her own state.

thinai_evidence.note: the threatened parting is what she answers

218.reading: The friend tells the lover, who said his eyes would not close except on her shoulders on nights when the storm cloud flashes and thunders over the peaks, after the tusker has fed sprouts and fodder to his herd, and who thinks it easy to come at midnight through the mountain clefts where the tiger waits for travellers, that if they cannot embrace his chest even one day they too will waste; let mother know and the old town gossip: let him come by day to the cool slope where vengai and thondri smell sweet.
218.nuance: Moving the meeting to daytime is a dare: the friend accepts the risk of discovery (let mother know, let the town hear) rather than his risk on the night path, which forces the matter toward marriage. She quotes his own lover's oath back to him before setting her terms.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகளை இடத்துய்த்து வந்து பகற்குறிநேர்ந்த வாய் பாட்டால் தலைமகனை வரைவுகடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend arranges a day meeting for the lovers

iraicchi.act: the tusker who cherishes his herd feeds them sprouts and the fodder they want
iraicchi.sense: as the tusker openly provides for his own, the lover should take up the care of the girl in marriage rather than steal visits by night

219.reading: The mother whose daughter has gone grieves that the girl who ran ringing her anklets through their great house and played ball with her friends, whom she fed from a bowl of milk like a white pakandrai flower brimming with dew ('drink your father's share too'), and adorned from birth, has gone with a heartless man; she cannot forget and wonders whether the girl walks, wasting, the long waterless road where a stag flees the red dog and the hot wind in the dry vila pods sounds to cowherds like a flute.
219.nuance: The feeding scene is told in the mother's own coaxing words, which makes the loss concrete: the voice that coaxed is still speaking, with no child to hear it. The flute that the cowherds imagine in the wind is the road's one sound of home, and it is false.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless road and the hot wind

comparisons.tenor: the wind in the dry vila pods

220.reading: The friend, meeting the lover as he leaves the night tryst, tells him that while gossip rises in town and street he goes about in his chariot and speaks humbly, shivering whenever he thinks of her body, unapproachable as the guarded pillar of the sacrifice the axe-bearing tall one completed at Chellur; he stands outside and suffers, and should instead, like the great bird at Oonur by the sea, settle in a steady union and speak the words that protect her beauty, so that they may be at ease.
220.nuance: The sacrificial pillar roped at its waist, which none may approach, makes the girl's guarded state a sacred enclosure that only a public rite can open: the friend is asking for marriage. Several phrases (நோலா இரும்புள், the whole of lines 10 to 21) are obscure and the reading is tentative.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிவந்து நீங்குச் தலைமகனை யெதிர்ப்பட்டுத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea tide, backwaters and shore grove

comparisons.tenor: the steady union the lover should enter

links.note: Both are a friend comforting a woman whose man has crossed the desert, and both argue that no gain could keep him: 201 says not even the Chola rice country, 213 not even the world of the worthy with its nectar.
links.teaches: Side by side they show the friend's reassurance as a scale that can be pushed from an earthly kingdom to heaven, always measuring his love by what he would refuse rather than by any promise he made.

links.note: 204 says the wife's hair smells of the groves of Vaanan's Sirukudi; 117 compares the eloping girl's braided hair to the ripples of the stream north of Vaanan's Sirukudi.
links.teaches: Two poets use the same chief's village to praise a woman's hair, one by its scent and one by its waves, so Vaanan's Sirukudi had become a standing measure of hair rather than a single poet's image.

links.note: Kural 1154 asks whether those who trusted the man who said 'fear not' are at fault if he leaves; in 205 the woman names his oath 'we will not part' a lie and yet wishes his journey success.
links.teaches: The couplet treats the broken promise as a question of blame, while the poem shows the same woman blaming and blessing him at once, so the trust the Kural judges was not withdrawn when it was betrayed.

links.note: Both are Paranar's and both tell of Aay Eyinan falling to Minjili: 181 has a flock of birds cover the sun over the dead man; 208 has Nannan refuse to look on the field where the birds shade him.
links.teaches: Together they show the bird-shade legend was told with a witness who would not look, so the poet could use the same event for wonder in a journey poem and for a ruler's shame in a love poem.

links.note: 36 (Nakkirar) and 209 (Kalladanar) both measure gossip against the victory roar at Alankanam, where the Pandya Chezhiyan beat seven kings in a day.
links.teaches: Two poets reached for the same Pandya victory to size two different scandals, a husband's new marriage and a girl's secret love, which shows the battle's roar had become a set unit of public noise in akam.

links.note: Purananuru 158 lists Ori who ruled Kolli and Malaiyan who rode the horse Kaari side by side among the seven dead givers; Akananuru 209 says Kaari of Mullur killed Ori and gave Kolli to the Cheras.
links.teaches: The bards' roll of the seven great givers sets a killer and his victim together as equals in generosity, and only the akam simile keeps the memory that one of them ended the other.

links.note: 226 names Mathi, lord of the fishermen, at the Kazhar ford where the Kaveri flooded; 211 names Mathi's stony ford and the gate of Venmani where Ezhini's teeth were set, and measures the gossip by the roar of its water.
links.teaches: Read together they show the akam poets drew their measures of public noise from the same Mathi's river country, one by a flood and the other by a war trophy, so a chief's ford could carry both his water and his fame.

links.note: Both answer a man who announces his departure: Kural 1151 says tell your quick return to those who will be alive then; 215 says wishing you a safe journey is for those who can bear to stay.
links.teaches: The poem shows how the couplet's refusal works in practice: the friend withholds the ritual farewell and fills the road with killers and vultures, so the threat of death the Kural only implies is made visible.

links.note: Purananuru 396 praises Ezhini Aathan of Vaattaaru as strength to the weak and kin to the kinless, in a land where the Kosar drink toddy; Akananuru 216 recalls the spear of the lord of Chelli, a Kosar town, pressed into Aathan Ezhini's chest.
links.teaches: If the two name the same chief, the patron the bard praised as a protector was remembered in akam only for his death wound, which a courtesan uses as a measure of how much she can hurt her rivals.

links.note: 202 counts the dangers of the lover's night path (thunder, snake, dark) to press for marriage; 218 counts the same dangers (tiger, night clefts) and moves the meeting to daytime instead.
links.teaches: Read in order they show the friend's two moves against the night meeting: first making the danger the women's suffering, then offering daylight, which trades his peril for the risk of the mother's knowing.

links.note: Both mothers recall feeding the girl milk at home, 219 coaxing her with 'your father's share too', 207 holding out milk with honey she refused, and both set it against the water of the desert road.
links.teaches: Two poets build the eloping daughter's mother around the same contrast of home milk and road water, so the feeding bowl was the stock emblem of the care the daughter left behind.

links.note: Both are Maruthan Ila Naganar's neythal poems naming Chellur: in 90 it is the town of the mighty god by the roaring sea, in 220 the place of the sacrifice of the axe-bearing tall one with its guarded pillar.
links.teaches: The same poet ties Chellur's sanctity once to its god and once to a famous sacrifice, so for him the town was a sacred place whose guarded objects could stand for a girl kept from her lover.

new_concepts.gloss: marriage as the end of secret love; the friend's pressing of the lover to marry (வரைவு கடாயது)
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons of 202 and 218 (வரைவு கடாயது, வரைவுகடாயது)

new_concepts.gloss: the appointed meeting place of secret lovers, by day (பகற்குறி) or by night (இரவுக்குறி)
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons of 202, 212, 218 and 220 (இரவுக் குறி, அல்லகுறி, பகற்குறி)

source_issues: 203: the colophon thurai reads 1தாய், a stray footnote numeral before தாய்.
207: the colophon thurai reads 4தாய், a stray footnote numeral before தாய்.
212: the colophon thurai has a stray numeral (1நெருங்கிச்) and breaks off without its verb (…நெஞ்சினை நெருங்கிச் with no சொல்லியது).

214: the colophon says தலைமகள் speaks to her heart in the war camp (பாசறைக்கண்), but the speaker is in the camp and says the war is ours (அமரும் நம்வயினதுவே) and wonders how she fares; it should be தலைமகன். thurai_akam is marked with the hero as speaker. Line 10 கொள் is likely a misprint for கொல்.
220: the colophon thurai reads நீங்குச், a misprint for நீங்கும்.
210: the colophon thurai splits சொல்லுவாளாய் as சொல்லு வாளாய்.
217: the base text has 20 lines and the commentary edition 19 (flagged); line 8 opens with a stray quotation mark ('தோலெறி) that is never closed.
206: line 2 has a stray exclamation mark inside the phrase (பெண்கொண்டு!), and line 15 splits யாஅங்கு as யா அங்கு.
219: line 1 ends with a full stop mid-sentence, and line 18 has a closing double quote with no opening one.
216: line 6 has a closing quotation mark (மொழிப') with no opening one.
